offices.officeName: Alaska Department of Health, Health Analytics and Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: There is no county office to fall back on: Anchorage and Juneau are the two counters in the state. A parent listed on the certificate may order; anyone who is not on it needs a notarized letter of consent. Orders are taken in person, by mail, by fax, and online through VitalChek.

offices.officeName: Alabama Department of Public Health, Center for Health Statistics
offices.orderingNote: Any county health department in Alabama can issue a certified copy of an Alabama birth certificate, most of them while you wait, so the nearest county office is usually faster than writing to Montgomery. The record is restricted: a parent named on it qualifies, and identification is required. VitalChek is the state's online and telephone channel.

offices.officeName: Arkansas Department of Health, Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: Arkansas offers vital records services in every county through its local health units, so a walk-in at the county unit is an alternative to the Little Rock office. An acceptable photo ID is required, and there is a mail application and a telephone line as well as online ordering.

offices.officeName: Arizona Department of Health Services, Bureau of Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: The state office in Phoenix takes requests in person, by mail and by phone, and VitalChek is its online channel. The page also points to the county health departments, which is worth checking for a recent birth.

offices.officeName: California Department of Public Health, Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: California issues both authorized certified copies and informational copies. Only the authorized copy establishes identity, and only a parent named on the record (or a short list of other relatives) may request one. The request has to carry a notarized sworn statement unless it is made in person. County recorders in the county of birth are usually faster than the state office for a recent birth.

offices.officeName: Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: Requests go to the state office in person or by mail, with VitalChek as the telephone and online channel. Several county public health agencies issue certified copies as well, which is usually the shorter route for a recent birth.

offices.officeName: Connecticut Department of Public Health, State Vital Records Office
offices.orderingNote: For a birth from 2003 onwards, any town vital records office in Connecticut can issue a certified copy, and the town is generally quicker than the state office. A valid government photo ID is required, or two documents from the state's alternative list. Eligibility runs to the parents, the person themselves at eighteen, and a short list of relatives.

offices.officeName: DC Health, Vital Records Division
offices.orderingNote: The District issues the long-form certificate only. Identification matching the name on the record is required, and orders are taken by mail, by phone and online through VitalChek.

offices.officeName: Delaware Division of Public Health, Office of Vital Statistics
offices.orderingNote: Delaware runs three walk-in locations as well as taking mailed requests at the Dover office, and it offers parents a way to pre-order a newborn's certificate rather than waiting to apply afterwards.

offices.officeName: Florida Department of Health, Bureau of Vital Statistics
offices.orderingNote: A Florida birth record stays confidential for 125 years: the parents named on it, the registrant at eighteen, and legal guardians or representatives qualify, and anybody else needs a notarized affidavit from somebody who does. Valid photo ID is required. County health departments issue records from 1917 onwards, which usually beats writing to Jacksonville. VitalChek is the online vendor.

offices.officeName: Georgia Department of Public Health, State Office of Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: Certified copies come from the county vital records office or from the state office, and the county is the shorter route. A parent ordering has to be named on the certificate and show a government photo ID carrying a signature. Georgia approves three online vendors rather than one.

offices.officeName: Hawaii Department of Health, Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: Hawaii takes orders through its own state portal rather than a third-party vendor, and a government-issued photo ID is required. There is an issuance office in Honolulu for anybody who can go in person.

offices.officeName: Iowa Department of Health and Human Services, Bureau of Health Statistics
offices.orderingNote: Iowa is the notarization state: unless the application is handed over in person it has to be notarized, and it needs a current government photo ID with it. County recorders act as local registrars and hold the records for births in their county.

offices.officeName: Idaho Department of Health and Welfare, Bureau of Vital Records and Health Statistics
offices.orderingNote: The bureau has no public counter, so a certified copy is ordered online or by mail rather than collected. Access is restricted to the person named, immediate family and anybody who can show a tangible interest.

offices.officeName: Illinois Department of Public Health, Division of Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: The person named on the record at eighteen, a parent shown on it, or a legal guardian or representative with written evidence may order. The state office takes requests in person, by mail, by phone and by email, and it publishes a directory of county clerks, who hold the local copy of a record filed in their county.

offices.officeName: Indiana Department of Health, Division of Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: The department says plainly that walk-in service is not available at the state office and that ordering through the local health department where the birth happened is faster. VitalChek is the only online vendor it authorizes.

offices.officeName: Kansas Department of Health and Environment, Office of Vital Statistics
offices.orderingNote: Copies go to the person named, immediate family, a legal representative, or somebody who can show a direct interest. Walk-in and mail requests go to Topeka, and the office contracts with a single vendor for internet orders.

offices.officeName: Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services, Office of Vital Statistics
offices.orderingNote: Orders are taken in person, by mail, through a drop box at the visitor entrance, and online through VitalChek, and a valid photo ID is needed to collect a will-call order. Kentucky's county and circuit clerks hold old marriage and divorce records, not birth records, so the state office is the route.

offices.officeName: Louisiana Department of Health, Vital Records Registry
offices.orderingNote: Louisiana is a closed-record state: a parent, the adult registrant, a sibling, a grandparent or a grandchild may order, and an attorney needs a written declaration of representation. Participating Clerks of Court around the state issue certified copies, and internet, fax and telephone orders go through VitalChek.

offices.officeName: Massachusetts Department of Public Health, Registry of Vital Records and Statistics
offices.orderingNote: Two places hold the record: the Registry in Dorchester holds the statewide copy and the city or town clerk holds the local one, and either can issue. A mailed request has to carry a photocopy of the requester's government photo ID.

offices.officeName: Maryland Department of Health, Division of Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: The person named, a parent named on the certificate, a court-appointed guardian, or a representative of one of them may order. Same-day service needs an unexpired government photo ID showing an issue and an expiry date; without one, two alternative documents are required instead.

offices.officeName: Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention, Division of Data, Research, and Vital Statistics
offices.orderingNote: Most municipal offices in Maine hold vital records as well as the state office, so the town office is worth trying before Augusta. Certified copies go to eligible applicants only.

offices.officeName: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services, Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: A Michigan birth record stays restricted for 100 years, so eligibility has to be shown rather than assumed: the person, a parent, a legal guardian or a representative. The state takes orders online and by mail, and the county clerk where the birth happened is the other route.

offices.officeName: Minnesota Department of Health, Office of Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: Minnesota releases a certified copy only to somebody with a tangible interest in the record, and the request has to be signed in front of a notary or in front of county vital records staff. County offices issue as well as the state.

offices.officeName: Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, Bureau of Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: Requests go to the Bureau of Vital Records in Jefferson City by mail or in person, and Missouri also issues many records through local public health agencies once the state has registered them.

offices.officeName: Mississippi State Department of Health, Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: Requests go to the Ridgeland office in person or by mail, by telephone, or online through the service the department contracts with.

offices.officeName: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services, Office of Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: Orders go to the Helena office by mail, or through the two vendors the office contracts with. It names them rather than leaving it open, so a site that is not one of the two is not the state's channel.

offices.officeName: North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, NC Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: The register of deeds in the county where the birth happened can usually issue a certified copy the same day, which is the fast route; the state office in Raleigh is the slower one.

offices.officeName: North Dakota Health and Human Services, Division of Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: North Dakota's list is short: the person named on the record, once they are sixteen, or a parent named on it. The state's own secure online application is the quickest channel.

offices.officeName: Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: Nebraska releases a certified copy to the person on the record and to applicants who can show a proper purpose, with a current government photo ID. Orders are taken online, by mail and in person in Lincoln.

offices.officeName: New Hampshire Department of State, Division of Vital Records Administration
offices.orderingNote: New Hampshire keeps vital records with the Secretary of State rather than with the health department, which is worth knowing before searching. City and town clerks issue certified copies as well as the Concord office, and an application needs photo identification with it.

offices.officeName: New Jersey Department of Health, Office of Vital Statistics and Registry
offices.orderingNote: A request has to carry proof of your relationship to the person on the record as well as a copy of your own ID. The local registrar of the municipality where the birth happened can issue in person; otherwise it is the state office in Trenton.

offices.officeName: New Mexico Department of Health, Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: New Mexico restricts access to the registrant, immediate family, and anybody with tangible proof of legal interest, and it lists exactly who counts as immediate family. The state does not take cards directly, so online orders go through VitalChek.

offices.officeName: Nevada Division of Public and Behavioral Health, Office of Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: Birth records are confidential in Nevada and go only to a qualified applicant: the registrant, a direct family member by blood or marriage, a guardian, or a legal representative. The state office issues birth records; the county recorders issue marriage records, which is a common wrong turn.

offices.officeName: New York State Department of Health, Bureau of Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: New York is two systems, and this is the one that does not cover New York City. A birth in Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx or Staten Island is a New York City Department of Health record and has to be ordered from the city, not from Albany. Everywhere else in the state is here.

offices.officeName: Ohio Department of Health, Bureau of Vital Statistics
offices.orderingNote: Any local health district in Ohio can issue a certified copy of any Ohio birth, not only of the ones registered in that district, and each district sets its own fee. The state office in Columbus takes mail orders.

offices.officeName: Oklahoma State Department of Health, Vital Records Service
offices.orderingNote: Every applicant has to send a copy of a government photo ID, and more may be asked for to show entitlement. Orders are taken online and by telephone, with will-call pickup for anybody who can get to the office.

offices.officeName: Oregon Health Authority, Center for Health Statistics
offices.orderingNote: Certified copies come from the county where the birth happened as well as from the state office, and counties commonly handle recent births. Orders are taken online, in person, by phone and by mail, and Oregon issues only to a qualified applicant.

offices.officeName: Pennsylvania Department of Health, Division of Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: Pennsylvania restricts a birth record for 105 years, so the applicant has to be eligible, show valid identification and sign the application. The Commonwealth authorizes exactly one online vendor, reached through its own health.pa.gov address.

offices.officeName: Rhode Island Department of Health, Center for Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: For a birth from 1960 onwards, any city or town clerk in Rhode Island can issue the certificate, as can the Center for Vital Records in Cranston. A valid government photo ID is required to show you are entitled to it.

offices.officeName: South Carolina Department of Public Health, Division of Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: Requests go to the Columbia office in person or by mail, or online through the state's vendor. County health departments issue a short-form birth card rather than the full certified copy, which is not always the document another office will accept.

offices.officeName: South Dakota Department of Health, Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: Certified copies can be collected in person at a county Register of Deeds office as well as from the Pierre office, and orders are also taken by mail, by phone and online.

offices.officeName: Tennessee Department of Health, Office of Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: Any county health department can issue any Tennessee birth certificate the state holds, so there is no need to travel to the county of birth. Identification is required when the application is handed over, and Tennessee authorizes a single card vendor for online orders.

offices.officeName: Texas Department of State Health Services, Vital Statistics
offices.orderingNote: Texas issues only to a properly qualified applicant, and it defines the term: the person, a parent, a spouse, a sibling, a child, a grandparent, a guardian, or a legal agent. The state runs its own ordering site, and the local registrar where the birth was registered is the other counter.

offices.officeName: Utah Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Vital Records and Statistics
offices.orderingNote: Certificates go to the person of record, immediate family, guardians and designated legal representatives, and a family member may be asked to prove the relationship with another certificate. Most Utah local health departments take in-person orders as well as the state office.

offices.officeName: Virginia Department of Health, Office of Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: Every request needs a legible copy of the requester's identification and a signature. Virginia is unusual in also issuing vital records at DMV customer service centres, which is often the quickest counter.

offices.officeName: Vermont Department of Health, Vital Records
offices.orderingNote: The town or city clerk is the cheapest and quickest route in Vermont and can issue certified copies going back to 1909; the state also sells certified copies online. Valid identification is required for a certified copy.

offices.officeName: Washington State Department of Health, Center for Health Statistics
offices.orderingNote: Local health jurisdictions and county offices issue as well as the state office, and an in-person request at either is often same-day. What each local office offers varies, so it is worth checking before driving.

offices.officeName: Wisconsin Department of Health Services, Vital Records Office
offices.orderingNote: Wisconsin county Register of Deeds offices issue birth records as well as the Madison office, and walk-in service in Madison is usually same-day. A mailed application needs a photocopy of an acceptable photo ID; VitalChek handles online and telephone orders.

offices.officeName: West Virginia Department of Health, Vital Registration Office
offices.orderingNote: In-person requests at the Charleston office are same-day. A mailed request needs a colour copy of your identification, and the office takes check or money order only. County clerks hold locally filed records.

offices.officeName: Wyoming Department of Health, Vital Statistics Services
offices.orderingNote: Certified copies go to the registrant, either parent named on the certificate, a legal guardian, or a lawyer for one of them. Wyoming runs its own online portal, with mail forms for anybody who cannot use it.
